facts.statement: The genus Kambara was described by Willis, Molnar, and Scanlon in 1993.
facts.quote: authority: Willis, Molnar & Scanlon, 1993

facts.statement: Kambara lived during the Eocene epoch.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Eocene,

facts.statement: Mature Kambara crocodilians generally reached lengths of 3 to 4 meters.
facts.quote: Kambara were medium-sized crocodilians, with mature specimens generally reaching lengths from 3-4 m.

facts.statement: The flattened skull shape and depositional environment suggest Kambara were semi-aquatic ambush predators.
facts.quote: The general shape of the skull, which is flattened, and the environment the fossils were deposited in, all suggest that they were semi-aquatic ambush predators like modern crocodilians.

facts.statement: Differences in limb bones suggest Kambara may have been better adapted for walking on land than modern Australian crocodiles.
facts.quote: However, subtle differences in the postcranial remains, especially the limb bones, suggest that Kambara may have been better adapted at walking on land than the two crocodile species still inhabiting Australia today, the saltwater and freshwater crocodile.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Kambara was fully terrestrial or simply better adapted for land than modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: While this could suggest that it was faster on land than living crocodilians, it does not necessarily mean that it was terrestrial like some later mekosuchines are thought to have been.

facts.statement: It is unclear how K. murgonensis and K. implexidens differed ecologically despite their anatomical differences.
facts.quote: It is unclear how exactly these two species differed in their niche, but they did differ notably in their anatomy, with the latter being slightly more gracile and with interlocking teeth.

facts.statement: Researchers debate whether K. murgonensis and K. implexidens coexisted or were driven together by drought.
facts.quote: It is also possible that the two species didn't coexist at all, but instead were driven together by drought.

facts.statement: Some studies suggest Kambara was not a mekosuchine, though this view is not supported by all authors.
facts.quote: Other studies suggest that Kambara was no mekosuchine at all, but said results are not supported by all authors.

facts.statement: Ralph Molnar first formally described Kambara material in 1982, initially identifying it as a Miocene crocodylid.
facts.quote: Although known for half a century, the material was first formally described by Ralph Molnar in 1982, who reported a lower jaw bone he believed to belong to a Miocene crocodylid.

facts.statement: Kambara taraina was named in 2009 by Lucas A. Buchanan.
facts.quote: The most recent addition to this genus was K. taraina, named in 2009 by Lucas A. Buchanan.

facts.statement: The first remains were found in the Oakdale Sandstone Formation near Murgon, Queensland.
facts.quote: the first remains found in rock units of what may be part of the Oakdale Sandstone Formation near the township of Murgon, Queensland.

facts.statement: The name Kambara derives from an Aboriginal word for crocodile within the Queensland language group.
facts.quote: the name Kambara is stated to derive from an Aboriginal word for crocodile, however, it is not specified which language in particular, only that it stems from the Queensland language group.

facts.statement: The name K. taraina derives from the Darumbal dialect and means crocodile.
facts.quote: The species name derives from the dialect of the Darumbal people and simply means crocodile.

facts.statement: Kambara had a typically crocodilian skull that was roughly triangular, starting narrow at the snout and widening towards the back.
facts.quote: The skull of Kambara appears typically crocodilian, being roughly triangular with a rostrum that begins relatively narrow and continues to widen towards the back.

facts.statement: The species K. murgonensis is described as having a moderately broad snout and a robust build.
facts.quote: K. murgonensis for instance is described as being moderately broad-snouted with a robust build.

facts.statement: The skull roof of Kambara was relatively flat without raised edges, but specimens show well-developed pits just before the supratemporal fenestrae.
facts.quote: The skull table of Kambara was relatively flat, lacking the raised edges seen in today's crocodiles, but instead multiple specimens across species show the presence of well developed pits just before the supratemporal fenestrae.

facts.statement: The species K. taraina had a long, high, and wide retroarticular process that provided a large surface area for muscle attachment.
facts.quote: K. taraina stands out as having a long, high and wide process, offering a greater surface area for the musculature to attach to.

facts.statement: Older species of Kambara had less developed retroarticular processes, with K. molnari having a long but narrow one and K. implexidens having a short and low one.
facts.quote: the retroarticular processes in older species are less well developed, with that of K. molnari being described as long but narrow, while that of K. implexidens was short and low.

facts.statement: Three distinct morphologies of the toothrow are observed in Kambara, primarily differing in how the upper and lower teeth interact.
facts.quote: Generally, three different morphologies can be observed, with the difference being primarily expressed through how the upper and lower toothrow interact with one another.

facts.statement: K. murgonensis had an overbite where upper jaw teeth overlapped lower jaw teeth, similar to an alligator.
facts.quote: In K. murgonensis, the teeth of the upper jaw overlap those of the lower jaw, giving it an overbite similar to that of an alligator.

facts.statement: In K. implexidens, the first lower jaw teeth slid into pronounced pits that pierced the upper jaw bones and emerged above the nostrils.
facts.quote: In K. implexidens, the first teeth of the lower jaw slide into very pronounced pits that pierce the bones of the upper jaw, emerging on its upper surface in front of the nostrils.

facts.statement: In K. taraina, teeth interlocked in the premaxilla, and the first dentary teeth extended into the bone without breaching the dorsal surface like in K. implexidens.
facts.quote: In K. taraina the teeth clearly interlock in the premaxilla as well, however, while the first pair of dentary teeth also extend into the bone, they do not breach the dorsal surface as in K. implexidens.

facts.statement: K. molnari displayed an intermediate dentition condition between the overbite of K. murgonensis and the extensive interlocking of K. implexidens.
facts.quote: The third type is observed in K. molnari, which shows a somewhat intermediate condition between the overbite of K. murgonensis and the more extensive interlocking dentition of K. implexidens.

facts.statement: All Kambara teeth were slightly compressed side-to-side with distinct cutting edges but were not ziphodont like some later mekosuchines.
facts.quote: All teeth are slightly compressed side to side and possess distinct carinae (cutting edges), but are not ziphodont like in some later mekosuchines.

facts.statement: K. taraina had the fewest upper jaw teeth, with only 14 on either side.
facts.quote: K. taraina has the lowest number of teeth in the maxillae (and thus throughout the upper jaw) with only 14 teeth on either side.

facts.statement: K. implexidens and K. murgonensis both had 16 teeth in each maxilla, while the number for K. molnari is unknown.
facts.quote: The number is unknown for K. molnari, while both K. implexidens and K. murgonensis possess 16 teeth in either maxilla.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Kambara contained 17 or 18 dentary teeth.
facts.quote: The lower jaw contains 17 or 18 dentary teeth.

facts.statement: The humerus of Kambara was much straighter than in modern crocodiles, with both articulating surfaces level to each other.
facts.quote: The humerus of Kambara meanwhile is much straighter, with both surfaces being level to each other.

facts.statement: The distal end of the Kambara humerus had a hexagonal profile.
facts.quote: The profile of the distal end is subsequently hexagonal.

facts.statement: Known postcranial elements of Kambara include shoulder blades, coracoids, arm bones, finger bones, pelvic bones, hindlimbs, and various vertebrae including nearly the entire cervical series.
facts.quote: Additional known elements of the postcranial skeleton include shoulder blades, coracoids, bones of the lower arm, finger bone, pelvic bones, hindlimbs as well as multiple parts of the spinal cord, including nearly the entire cervical series, several dorsal and tail vertebrae as well as lumbar vertebrae in articulation.

facts.statement: The holotype of K. implexidens was estimated at 2.5 meters, while a larger mandible suggests lengths up to 3.5 meters.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of K. implexidens, which may be a subadult, has been estimated to have been 2.5 m, while a much larger mandible suggests lengths of up to 3.5 m.

facts.statement: K. molnari was described as reaching lengths between 3 and 4 meters.
facts.quote: The same applies to K. molnari, which was described as reaching lengths from 3-4 m.

facts.statement: Some phylogenetic analyses propose that Kambara is an early diverging crocodyloid and the sister taxon to the family Crocodylidae, rather than a mekosuchine.
facts.quote: these trees recover Kambara as an early diverging crocodyloid and immediate sister to Crocodylidae

facts.statement: Authors of certain studies consider the nodal support for the hypothesis that Mekosuchinae is a paraphyletic group to be poor.
facts.quote: nodal support for paraphyletic Mekosuchinae is considered to be poor by the authors

facts.statement: Kambara is generally considered to have been a semi-aquatic generalist with an appearance resembling modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: it is generally thought that Kambara was a semi-aquatic generalist

facts.statement: Charles C. Mook hypothesized that the overbite in crocodilians functioned similarly to mammalian carnassial teeth for breaking and slicing prey.
facts.quote: One hypothesis by Charles C. Mook proposed that an overbite in crocodilians could serve a similar function as the carnassial teeth of mammalian predators

facts.statement: The strong bite of K. taraina suggests it could hunt larger, more terrestrial prey, while older species likely fed on smaller animals.
facts.quote: This may suggest that K. taraina was capable of taking on larger, more terrestrial prey items, whereas older species fed on smaller animals

facts.statement: Multiple Kambara species exhibit well-defined muscle attachment sites used for holding and crushing prey, an activity not primarily performed by the pterygoid muscles.
facts.quote: multiple species of Kambara show well defined attachment sites for musculature used to hold and crush prey

facts.statement: Recent phylogenetic studies identify K. implexidens as the most basal species of Kambara, while K. molnari is often excluded due to limited fossil material.
facts.quote: Recent phylogenies consistently point towards K. implexidens as the basal most species of Kambara, although K. molnari is typically removed due to the limited nature of its material

facts.statement: A fossil plastron of Kambara displays circular pits arranged linearly that match the bite marks of a crocodilian.
facts.quote: The fossil, a nearly complete plastron, shows several circular pits arranged in a linear fashion, which is in line with the bite marks left by a crocodilian.

facts.statement: Researchers believe the crocodile that bit a Kambara fossil was overambitious because the plastron's width and thickness were too great for an average Kambara individual to swallow.
facts.quote: However, it is believed that in this instance the crocodile was overambitious, as the plastron's width and thickness would be too great for the average Kambara individual to manage.

facts.statement: After being bitten by a crocodile, a Kambara fossil showed signs of healing but later died from infection and necrosis.
facts.quote: Subsequently, the turtle was let go or escaped the crocodile, allowing the bite to somewhat heal. Despite this however, the turtle later died from infection and necrosis.

facts.statement: While Kambara fossils show evidence of being preyed upon by crocodiles, this does not necessarily mean Kambara was specialized for hunting turtles.
facts.quote: While this suggests that turtles, which were a readily available food source, were fed on at least occasionally, it does not necessarily mean that Kambara was specialised for hunting them.

facts.statement: Changes to Kambara's deltapectoral crest could have provided advantages for swimming by allowing limbs to better resist drag during the recovery stroke.
facts.quote: The change to the deltapectoral crest could have advantages for swimming, allowing the limbs to better resist the drag during the recovery stroke.

facts.statement: The genus Kambara was described by Willis et al. in 1993.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Willis et al., 1993

facts.statement: Four species of Kambara are known: K. murgonensis (type species, Willis et al., 1993), K. implexidens (Salisbury & Willis, 1996), K. molnari (Holt et al., 2005), and K. taraina (Buchanan, 2009).
facts.quote: subdivision: K. murgonensis Willis et al., 1993 (tipo) K. implexidens Salisbury & Willis, 1996 K. molnari Holt et al., 2005 K. taraina Buchanan, 2009

facts.statement: Kambara was an extinct Mekosuchine crocodilian that lived during the Eocene and Oligocene periods in present-day Australia.
facts.quote: Kambara es un género extinto de crocodiliano mekosuquino que vivió durante los períodos Eoceno y Oligoceno en la actual Australia.

facts.statement: With an age of approximately 55 million years, Kambara fossils are among the oldest Tertiary fossils found in Australia.
facts.quote: Con cerca de 55 millones de años de antigüedad, los restos de Kambara están entre los más antiguos fósiles del Terciario hallados en Australia

facts.statement: Kambara is the oldest known Mekosuchine.
facts.quote: Kambara es el más antiguo mekosuquino conocido.

facts.statement: All four species of Kambara share a body plan typical of crocodilians and grew to sizes similar to the modern saltwater crocodile, Crocodylus porosus.
facts.quote: Todas las cuatro especies comparten un plan corporal propio de cualquier crocodiliano, creciendo hasta tamaños similares al del moderno cocodrilo de agua salada, Crocodylus porosus.

facts.statement: Kambara exhibits the interesting characteristic of having multiple bite patterns within the same genus.
facts.quote: Kambara muestra la interesante característica de tener múltiples patrones de mordida dentro del mismo género.

facts.statement: K. murgonensis has an almost complete overbite, K. implexidens has interlocking dentition, and K. molnari has an intermediate condition.
facts.quote: Kambara murgonensis tiene una sobremordida casi completa, K. implexidens tiene una dentición entrelazada y K. molnarai una condición intermedia.

facts.statement: Fossils of this genus have been found at the Murgon fossil site in southeast Queensland.
facts.quote: Fósiles de este género se ahn hallado en el sitio fósil Murgon en el sureste de Queensland.

facts.statement: Fossils of K. implexidens were found near Murgon, Queensland, alongside fossils of K. murgonensis.
facts.quote: Los fósiles de K. implexidens se encontraron junto a los de K. murgonensis en la zona de la montaña del barco, cerca de Murgon, Queensland

facts.statement: K. implexidens was not recognized as a distinct species until nearly complete skulls were discovered in 1993.
facts.quote: K. implexidens no fue reconocida como una especie distinta hasta el descubrimiento de cráneos casi completos en 1993

facts.statement: The teeth of K. implexidens interlock rather than forming an overbite.
facts.quote: los dientes de K. implexidens se entrelazan, en lugar de formar una sobremordida

facts.statement: The skull of K. implexidens was relatively gracile, as were its teeth.
facts.quote: el cráneo de esta especie era relativamente más grácil, al igual que sus dientes

facts.statement: K. molnari is known from a partial jaw and several isolated remains collected from the Rundle Formation.
facts.quote: K. molnari, se conoce a partir de una mandíbula parcial y varios restos aislados, todos recolectados de la Formación Rundle

facts.statement: The teeth of K. molnari appear intermediate between the overbite of K. murgonensis and the interlocking dentition of K. implexidens and K. taraina.
facts.quote: los dientes parecen ser intermedios entre la sobremordida de K. murgonensis y la dentición entrelazada de K. implexidens y K. taraina

facts.statement: K. molnari was named in honor of Ralph Molnar for his constant contributions to mekosuchin research.

facts.statement: Remains of K. murgonensis were part of the Tingamarra fauna and found in areas overlapping the Oakdale Sandstone Formation.

facts.statement: K. murgonensis was a moderately robust animal with a skull much wider than that of the contemporary K. implexidens.
facts.quote: Era un animal moderadamente robusto con un cráneo mucho más ancho que el del contemporáneo K. implexidens

facts.statement: The species name K. taraina derives from the Darumbal people's dialect and simply means crocodile.

facts.statement: Kambara lived from the Ypresian to the Priabonian, between 56 and 33.9 million years ago.

facts.statement: Some phylogenetic analyses recover Kambara as an early-diverging crocodyloid and the sister taxon to Crocodylidae, excluding it from Mekosuchinae.

facts.statement: Recent phylogenies consistently point to K. implexidens as the most basal species of Kambara, although K. molnari is often excluded due to limited material.
